blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 18 (Inheritance), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe Mendel's monohybrid cross for seed shape and explain its results in terms of alleles and the law of segregation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The cross: Mendel crossed a true-breeding round-seeded pea plant with a wrinkled-seeded plant. All F1 plants produced round seeds, so round is dominant and wrinkled (not expressed in F1) is recessive. When F1 plants were self-pollinated, 1/4 of the F2 seeds were wrinkled: 3 dominant : 1 recessive. This 3:1 was a disguised 1:2:1 (1/4 pure-breeding dominant, 2/4 not pure-breeding dominant, 1/4 pure-breeding recessive).

Interpretation: characters are controlled by 'factors' (genes). Each individual is diploid with two genes for a character; the alternative forms of a gene are alleles. Same alleles = homozygous (RR, rr); different alleles = heterozygous (Rr), in which only the dominant allele is expressed.

Law of segregation: when an individual forms gametes, each gamete receives just one allele, selected randomly. So the F1 (Rr) forms R and r gametes; their random union gives 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, i.e. 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

book_ref.quote: When he crossed a true-breeding round-seeded plant with wrinkled-seeded plant

blocks.prompt: 2 Mendel's ideas were later linked with chromosomes. (i) State the chromosomal theory of inheritance and name the scientists linked with it. (ii) Explain the testcross with the example of seed shape. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Chromosomal theory (1 mark): in 1900 Karl Correns rediscovered Mendel's work and suggested the role of chromosomes in heredity; in 1902 Walter Sutton proposed the theory: genes are found at specific locations on chromosomes, and the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis explains Mendel's laws.

(ii) Testcross (3 marks): it is used to find whether a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous, by crossing it with a recessive phenotype. A round-seeded plant may be RR or Rr, while a wrinkled plant is always rr. The round plant is crossed with rr:
• If it is RR, it gives only R gametes, so all offspring are round (Rr).
• If it is Rr, it gives R and r gametes, so offspring are round (Rr) and wrinkled (rr) in a 1:1 ratio.
Thus the offspring reveal the unknown genotype.

book_ref.quote: A round-seeded plant may be RR (homozygous) or Rr (heterozygous)

blocks.prompt: 3 Independent assortment does not always hold. (i) Explain how independent assortment acts as a source of variations. (ii) Describe its limitations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Source of variations (2 marks): independent assortment mixes alleles during gamete formation; alleles for different traits on different chromosomes separate independently, so one character (eye colour) does not affect another (hair texture). It happens because homologous chromosome pairs line up randomly during meiosis, giving different combinations of maternal and paternal alleles; in humans over 8 million (2²³) combinations in one gamete, making every gamete unique. Fertilization combines unique gametes into a unique zygote, and this mixing creates genetic diversity that helps species adapt.

(ii) Limitations (2 marks):
1. Linked genes: genes close together on the same chromosome are often inherited together (gene linkage).
2. Chromosome crossover: exchange of material between homologous chromosomes in meiosis changes the predicted ratio.
3. Epistasis: one gene's effect is modified or suppressed by unrelated genes.
4. Pleiotropy: one gene controls multiple characters and can distort expected ratios.
5. Environmental effect: many phenotypes are affected by the environment.

book_ref.quote: This random alignment causes different combinations of maternal and paternal alleles in gametes

blocks.prompt: 4 A pea plant RrYy (round yellow) is crossed with a plant Rryy (round green), and 480 seeds are obtained. Using the product rule, find the expected number of each phenotype. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Treat each gene separately, then multiply the independent probabilities (product rule) and multiply by 480.

book_ref.quote: In a F1 dihybrid plant (RrYy), seed shape has alleles R, r and seed colour has Y, y

steps: Seed shape, Rr × Rr: P(round) = 3/4, P(wrinkled) = 1/4.
Seed colour, Yy × yy: gametes Y, y × y, so P(yellow, Yy) = 1/2, P(green, yy) = 1/2.
Wrinkled yellow = (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8; wrinkled green = (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8.
blocks.final_answer: 180 round yellow, 180 round green, 60 wrinkled yellow, 60 wrinkled green (ratio 3:3:1:1).

blocks.prompt: 5 In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three genes assorting independently), find the probability of an offspring that is (a) AABBCC, (b) aabbcc, (c) AaBbCc. Use the product rule, and the sum rule where needed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: For each gene find the probability from a one-gene cross, then multiply for the three independent genes.

book_ref.quote: So, probability of round yellow offspring = (3/4) × (3/4) = 9/16

steps: For one gene, Aa × Aa: each parent gives A or a with probability 1/2.
P(Aa): A from male + a from female, or a from male + A from female; by the sum rule 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

blocks.prompt: 6 Explain co-dominance with reference to the human MN blood group system, giving its alleles, genotypes, antigens and phenotypes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Co-dominance: both alleles of a gene pair are fully expressed in a heterozygous individual, without blending or one masking the other, so the products of both alleles appear together in the heterozygote's phenotype.

MN system: it has two alleles, Lᴹ (produces M antigen) and Lᴺ (produces N antigen). 'L' stands for Landsteiner and Levine, who discovered the system in 1927. It is also called the MNS system because the MN genes and the S/s genes are linked on the same chromosome.

Since Lᴹ and Lᴺ are co-dominant, both antigens appear on the RBCs when both alleles are present. Three possibilities:

book_ref.quote: The human MN blood group shows codominance, where both alleles are equally expressed

blocks.prompt: 7 The ABO system is a multiple allelic system. (i) What is a multiple allelic system? Name the alleles of the ABO system. (ii) Explain the principle of transfusion in the ABO system with its exceptions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (1 mark) A multiple allelic system occurs when a gene has more than two alleles in a population, creating more variation. The ABO system is controlled by gene I (on chromosome 9) with three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i; each person has only two of them.

(ii) (3 marks) Each group's plasma has antibodies against the antigen it lacks: A has anti-B, B has anti-A, AB has neither, O has both. In a transfusion between incompatible groups the recipient's antibodies attack the antigens on the donor's RBCs, causing clumping (agglutination). This happens:
• if a group A person receives group B blood and vice versa;
• if the donor is AB and the recipient is A, B or O.
Exceptions:
• O donor: has no antigen-A or antigen-B, so it can be given to A, B, AB or O (universal donor of the ABO system).
• AB recipient: has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so it can receive all types (universal recipient of the ABO system).

book_ref.quote: During blood transfusions between two incompatible (unmatching) blood groups

blocks.prompt: 8 A woman of blood group AB marries a man of blood group B whose mother was of blood group O. Find the man's genotype and the expected blood groups of their children with the probability of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the man's genotype from his mother, write the gametes and combine them.

book_ref.quote: The Iᴬ allele produces antigen-A, the Iᴮ allele produces antigen-B

steps: The man's mother was O (ii), so she gave him allele i; being group B he is Iᴮi.
Woman AB = IᴬIᴮ: gametes Iᴬ and Iᴮ (1/2 each). Man Iᴮi: gametes Iᴮ and i (1/2 each).
IᴬIᴮ (AB) = 1/4; Iᴬi (A) = 1/4; IᴮIᴮ (B) = 1/4; Iᴮi (B) = 1/4.
By the sum rule, P(B) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2; no child can be O, since the mother has no i.
blocks.final_answer: Man Iᴮi. Children: AB 1/4, A 1/4, B 1/2, O 0.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the Rh blood group system: its discovery, inheritance, and the principle of transfusion in the Rh system. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Discovery: the Rh system is the second most important blood group system in humans. Its name comes from the Rhesus monkey, in which Landsteiner first discovered its antigen in the 1930s. It is based on the presence (Rh-positive) or absence (Rh-negative) of the Rh-antigen (Rh factor or antigen-D) on RBCs. A blood group names both systems, e.g. A-positive or A-negative.

Inheritance: controlled by gene D with two alleles. The dominant D forms the Rh-antigen; the recessive d does not. So DD and Dd are Rh-positive and dd is Rh-negative.

Transfusion: unlike anti-A and anti-B, anti-Rh antibodies are not naturally present in Rh-negative people. If an Rh-negative person receives Rh-positive blood, his body starts producing anti-Rh antibodies, which destroy the donated RBCs and stay in the body for life. Hence O-negative (no ABO or Rh antigen) is the actual universal donor and AB-positive (no anti-A, anti-B or anti-Rh) the actual universal recipient.

book_ref.quote: It is the second most important blood group system in humans

blocks.prompt: 10 An Rh-negative woman marries an Rh-positive man. Find the chance that a child is Rh-positive (at risk of erythroblastosis foetalis) when the man is (a) DD, (b) Dd. In case (b), what is the chance that all three of their children are Rh-negative? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Write the woman's genotype, cross with each possible genotype of the man, then use the product rule for three independent births.

book_ref.quote: The dominant allele D forms the Rh-antigen

steps: The Rh-negative woman is dd; all her eggs carry d.
(a) DD × dd: all sperms carry D, so every child is Dd (Rh-positive): chance 1 (100%).
(b) Dd × dd: sperms D or d (1/2 each), so children Dd (Rh-positive) 1/2 and dd (Rh-negative) 1/2.
Three independent children all dd: (1/2) × (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/8.

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the complications that erythroblastosis foetalis causes in the foetus and new-born, and explain how ABO incompatibility can sometimes protect the baby. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cause in brief: an Rh-negative mother (dd) carrying an Rh-positive baby makes anti-Rh antibodies after foetal blood enters her blood; these cross the placenta and destroy foetal RBCs.

Complications:
1. Haemolytic anaemia and other serious complications in the foetus.
2. In severe cases, miscarriage or stillbirth.
3. If the foetus survives, the liver and spleen become enlarged as they try to make more RBCs.
4. Breakdown of RBCs produces bilirubin, which builds up and causes jaundice (yellow skin and eyes).
5. High bilirubin can damage brain cells.
The surviving baby's blood is replaced by Rh-negative blood free of anti-Rh antibodies.

Protection by ABO incompatibility: if an O-negative mother conceives an A-positive or B-positive baby, foetal RBCs entering her blood are quickly destroyed by her already present anti-A or anti-B antibodies, before she can form anti-Rh antibodies.

book_ref.quote: In severe cases, destruction of foetal RBCs can cause miscarriage or stillbirth

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe polygenic inheritance with the example of human skin colour. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Polygenic inheritance: polygenic characters are controlled by many gene pairs. All alleles of these genes contribute to the same trait in an additive way (some increase, some decrease the effect), and the combined effect produces a single trait with continuous variation (e.g. height, skin colour, weight, intelligence).

Skin colour: it depends on the amount of melanin; more melanin gives darker skin. It is controlled by about 60 genes, but for understanding three genes A, B, C are taken. Alleles A, B, C produce more melanin; a, b, c produce less.
• AABBCC (very dark) × aabbcc (very light) gives all AaBbCc children of intermediate colour.
• AaBbCc × AaBbCc gives a wide range from very dark to very light in the ratio 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1.
AABBCC is darkest (maximum melanin) and aabbcc lightest (minimum melanin); the many intermediate classes give continuous variation.

book_ref.quote: Skin colour depends on the amount of melanin pigment

blocks.prompt: 13 Using the three-gene model of skin colour, a person AaBbCc marries a person aabbcc. Find the kinds of children by number of dark alleles (A, B, C) and their ratio. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The aabbcc parent gives only abc gametes, so a child's dark alleles all come from the AaBbCc parent's gamete.

book_ref.quote: AABBCC → darkest (maximum melanin)

steps: AaBbCc forms 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 kinds of gametes, each with probability 1/8.
3 dark alleles (ABC): 1 gamete → 1/8.
2 dark alleles (ABc, AbC, aBC): 3 gametes → 3/8; 1 dark allele (Abc, aBc, abC): 3 gametes → 3/8.
0 dark alleles (abc): 1 gamete → 1/8. Total 1/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 1.
blocks.final_answer: Four classes, 3 : 2 : 1 : 0 dark alleles in the ratio 1 : 3 : 3 : 1; none is as dark as AABBCC.

blocks.prompt: 14 Gene interactions may be allelic or non-allelic. (i) Distinguish allelic and non-allelic interactions with examples. (ii) Explain the Bombay phenotype as an example of how one gene affects the expression of ABO genes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (2 marks) Most traits appear due to interactions between genes. In allelic interactions, alleles of the same gene interact (incomplete dominance, co-dominance, multiple alleles). In non-allelic interactions, alleles of different genes at different loci interact; a common example is epistasis, in which an epistatic allele masks or modifies the effect of hypostatic alleles of another gene.

(ii) (2 marks) Bombay phenotype: the expression of ABO genotypes depends on another gene, H, which makes H substance, the precursor of the A and B antigens. The Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles produce enzymes that modify H substance into antigen-A and antigen-B. A person with Iᴬ and Iᴮ but genotype hh makes no H substance, so no A or B antigens form and he has the O phenotype. It was discovered in Bombay in 1952 and is mostly found in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Iran.

book_ref.quote: The expression of ABO genotypes also depends upon another gene i.e., H

blocks.prompt: 15 A black Labrador BbEe is crossed with a yellow Labrador Bbee. Find the expected ratio of black, brown and yellow puppies. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the probability for each gene separately, then combine them using the epistasis rule: any ee dog is yellow.

book_ref.quote: When two heterozygous black dogs (BbEe × BbEe) are crossed

steps: Gene B, Bb × Bb: P(B_, black pigment) = 3/4, P(bb, brown pigment) = 1/4.
Gene E, Ee × ee: P(Ee, pigment deposited) = 1/2, P(ee, yellow) = 1/2.

blocks.prompt: 16 A white-flowered foxglove plant DdWw is crossed with a light red plant ddww. Find the expected ratio of white, dark red and light red flowers. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: ddww gives only dw gametes, so the offspring are decided by the four gametes of DdWw; any plant with W is white.

book_ref.quote: The heterozygous plant DdWw will have white flowers

steps: DdWw gametes: DW, Dw, dW, dw (1/4 each); ddww gametes: dw only.
Offspring: DdWw, Ddww, ddWw, ddww, each 1/4.
DdWw and ddWw have W, which limits pigment to small spots: white = 2/4.
Ddww: D with uniform pigment = dark red (1/4); ddww: light red (1/4).

blocks.prompt: 17 Explain how gene linkage is detected by crosses, distinguishing unlinked genes, incomplete linkage and complete linkage. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Background: thousands of genes lie on a limited number of chromosomes (humans about 20,000 genes on 23 chromosomes; Drosophila about 13,000 on 4), so many genes lie in a line on each chromosome. Genes on the same chromosome are linked; closely linked genes stay together, while genes on different chromosomes or far apart assort independently.

Detection: crosses are performed and the frequency of phenotypes in the offspring is observed. Parental combinations (same as the parents) are compared with recombinant (new) combinations. Linkage can be observed only with a large number of offspring; the larger the progeny, the closer it is to the actual frequency.
1. Parental and new phenotypes in an equal 1:1:1:1 ratio: genes are not linked and assort independently.
2. Parental combinations more frequent, new combinations fewer: incomplete linkage; genes are linked but can separate by crossing over.
3. Only parental combinations, no new ones: complete linkage; genes are very close and do not separate.

book_ref.quote: Gene linkage and its frequency can be studied by performing crosses

blocks.prompt: 18 Describe the process of crossing over and explain its significance. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Process:
1. During the formation of gametes (meiosis-I), homologous chromosomes go through crossing over.
2. The chromatids of the two homologous chromosomes line up next to one another.
3. They swap (exchange) sections of DNA; the DNA strands actually break and re-join.
4. After crossing over, the homologous chromosomes separate from each other.
5. The chromatids involved still have the same genes in the same order, but the alleles have been rearranged.

Significance:
• It is responsible for the recombination of linked genes, so linked genes can separate (incomplete linkage).
• Recombinant chromatids distributed in different gametes produce a wide variety of gametes.
• It therefore leads to recombination of genes and is responsible for genetic variability; it is also why gene-combination ratios may differ from those predicted by independent assortment.

book_ref.quote: During crossing over, the chromatids of two homologous chromosomes line up next to one another

blocks.prompt: 19 Sex is determined on the basis of karyotype. (i) Define karyotype, autosomes and sex chromosomes. (ii) Explain homogametic and heterogametic sexes with reference to humans, grasshopper and birds. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (2 marks) Karyotype is the appearance of the complete set of chromosomes in the cells, including their numbers, sizes and shapes. In most animals all pairs are similar in female and male except one. The chromosomes perfectly similar in both are autosomes; the one pair that differs and determines gender are the sex chromosomes.

(ii) (2 marks)
• Humans (XX-XY): females are homogametic, producing all eggs with one X; males are heterogametic, producing half X-sperms and half Y-sperms. X-sperm + egg = XX female; Y-sperm + egg = XY male.
• Grasshopper (XX-XO): the female (XX, 24 chromosomes) gives all eggs with X; the male (XO, 23 chromosomes) gives half X-sperms and half nullo sperms (no sex chromosome). X-sperm gives XX female; nullo sperm gives XO male.
• Birds (ZW-ZZ): the female (ZW) is heterogametic, producing Z eggs and W eggs; the male (ZZ) gives all Z sperms. Z egg gives a male; W egg gives a female.

book_ref.quote: On the other hand, males are heterogametic which means that they produce two types of sperm

blocks.prompt: 20 What is embryonic screening? Describe the procedure of amniocentesis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Embryonic screening: the methods to check genetic disorders and abnormal numbers of chromosomes in embryos. It includes ultrasound scan, chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis.

Amniocentesis:
1. It is generally done between the 15th and 20th week of pregnancy.
2. A long needle is inserted into the amniotic sac.
3. During this, an ultrasound probe locates the foetus and tests any abnormality.
4. The inserted needle sucks some amniotic fluid, which contains cells of the foetus.
5. The foetal cells are kept in a culture medium and checked for an abnormal number of chromosomes.

book_ref.quote: Embryonic screening are the methods to check genetic disorders and abnormal number of chromosomes in embryos

blocks.prompt: 21 Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A colour-blind man marries a woman of normal vision who is a carrier. Find the expected phenotypes of their sons and daughters with probabilities. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Write the alleles on the X chromosome (Xᶜ = colour-blind, X = normal); the Y carries no allele. Sons get the mother's X; daughters get one X from each parent.

book_ref.quote: So, this trait will appear in all the males who possess its allele

steps: Man XᶜY: sperms Xᶜ and Y (1/2 each). Carrier woman XXᶜ: eggs X and Xᶜ (1/2 each).
Daughters (get Xᶜ from father): XXᶜ carrier with normal vision 1/2; XᶜXᶜ colour-blind 1/2.
Sons (get Y from father): XY normal 1/2; XᶜY colour-blind 1/2.
Overall, 1/2 of all children are colour-blind (one allele is enough in sons, two are needed in daughters).
blocks.final_answer: Daughters: 1/2 carriers (normal), 1/2 colour-blind. Sons: 1/2 normal, 1/2 colour-blind.

blocks.prompt: 22 Describe the inheritance of X-linked dominant traits and Y-linked traits in humans, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
X-linked dominant traits:
• Examples: vitamin D-resistant rickets (softening and weakening of bones), Rett syndrome (loss of speech, repetitive hand movements, walking problems), Aicardi syndrome (abnormal brain development).
• An affected heterozygous mother passes the trait to 50% of her offspring (a homozygous mother to all).
• An affected father passes it to all his daughters (they inherit his X) and to none of his sons (they do not inherit his X).
• So these traits are more common in females, who have two X chromosomes.

Y-linked traits:
• The Y chromosome has relatively few genes compared with X, so Y-linked traits are rare.
• Their genes have no alleles on X and are called holandric (hemizygous) genes; they lie only on the non-homologous region of Y.
• They appear only in males and pass from father to son only.
• Examples: hypertrichosis (hair on the rim of the pinna), porcupine man (straight hair on the body), webbing of toes.

book_ref.quote: Such traits are in equal ratio in females and males

blocks.prompt: 23 Describe the mechanism of normal blood clotting. Name the types of haemophilia with the clotting factor and mode of inheritance of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Normal blood clotting:
1. At an injury, platelets adhere to the site and form a platelet plug.
2. Activated platelets and the damaged tissue release clotting factors.
3. The clotting factors perform chemical reactions (clotting cascade) in which soluble fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin.
4. Fibrin forms a mesh that entraps parts of the blood and makes a solid clot.
5. The clot is stabilized by cross-linking of fibrin strands.
If the balance is disrupted, abnormal clotting (thrombosis) can cause stroke and heart attack.

Haemophilia: the blood fails to clot properly after an injury due to reduction, malfunctioning or absence of clotting factors. Types:

book_ref.quote: Blood clotting is a complex process that helps to prevent excessive bleeding when an injury occurs

rows: X-linked recessive; more common in males
X-linked recessive; more common in males

blocks.prompt: 24 Describe trichromatic vision and the types of colour blindness (dichromacy and monochromacy). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Trichromatic vision: in people with normal vision the retina has three kinds of cone cells, each sensitive to a primary colour: red-, green- and blue-sensitive cones. Each contains its specific pigment proteins, opsins. The genes for red and green opsins are on the X chromosome; the gene for blue opsin is on autosome 7. Recessive alleles for opsins cause colour blindness.

Dichromacy: perception of two primary colours and blindness of the third, whose opsin is missing:
• red-blindness (protanopia)
• green blindness (deuteranopia)
• blue-blindness (tritanopia)
Red-green colour blindness is the common form in which the red or green opsin is missing or abnormal.

Monochromacy (total colour blindness): perception of a single colour and blindness of two colours whose opsins are missing. In blue-cone monochromacy the red and green opsins are absent; red-cone and green-cone monochromacy are very rare.

There is no cure; colour-blind glasses, special software and colour discrimination training help.

book_ref.quote: These are red-sensitive cones, green-sensitive cones and blue-sensitive cones

blocks.prompt: 25 Describe Duchenne muscular dystrophy: its inheritance, cause, course of the disease and management. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Inheritance: there are more than 30 muscular dystrophies; Duchenne is the most common. It is X-linked recessive, so more common in males. About two thirds of cases are inherited from the mother; one third are due to a new mutation.

Cause: a male who receives the recessive allele cannot make the muscle protein dystrophin. Muscle fibres die, and skeletal muscles weaken and break down, especially of the hips, pelvic area, thighs and calves; it later progresses to the shoulders and neck, arms, respiratory and cardiac muscles.

Course: it affects a child around the age of four and becomes evident when the child begins walking. By age 10 the child may need braces; by age 12 most patients cannot walk and need a wheelchair. Typical lifespans range from 15 to 45.

Management (no cure): physical therapy maintains strength, flexibility and mobility; corticosteroids give short-term improvement in muscle strength; pain-killers relieve muscle pain; surgery corrects joint contractures.

book_ref.quote: There are more than 30 disorders classified as muscular dystrophies
